title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXIII
paragraphs: These little things are great to little man.—GOLDSMITH.
“Have you seen much lately of that scientific marvel of yours, Lydgate?” Mr. Toller asked Mr. Farebrother, seated on his right at one of his Christmas dinner parties.
“Very little, I’m sorry to say,” the Vicar replied. He was used to fending off Toller’s teasing about his faith in the new medical star. “I live out of the way, and he’s too busy.”
“Is he? How glad I am to hear it,” said Dr. Minchin, blending smooth politeness with surprise.

“He spends a great deal of time at the New Hospital,” Farebrother continued. He had reasons for pursuing the subject. “My neighbor Mrs. Casaubon tells me about it. She visits often. She says Lydgate works tirelessly and is making something excellent of Bulstrode’s institution. He’s getting a new ward ready in case cholera reaches us.”
“And getting his theories of treatment ready to test on the patients, I imagine,” Toller said.

“Come now, Toller, be fair,” said Farebrother. “You’re much too clever not to recognize the value of a bold, fresh mind in medicine as in everything else. As for cholera, I suspect none of you is particularly certain what to do. If a man ventures a little too far down a new road, he generally does himself more harm than anyone else.”
“You and Wrench certainly ought to be grateful,” Dr. Minchin said, looking at Toller. “He’s sent you the best of Peacock’s patients.”
“Lydgate lives very extravagantly for a young man just starting out,” remarked Mr. Harry Toller, the brewer. “I suppose his family in the North supports him.”

“I hope they do,” said Mr. Chichely. “Otherwise he had no business marrying that lovely girl we were all so fond of. Damn it, you can’t help resenting a fellow who carries off the prettiest girl in town.”
“And the best, by God!” Mr. Standish added.

“My friend Vincy wasn’t at all pleased with the marriage, I know that,” Chichely said. “_He_ wouldn’t contribute much. I couldn’t say what the relatives on the other side may have put up.” His way of speaking made a point of seeming to withhold something.
“Oh, I shouldn’t think Lydgate ever expected to earn his living from his practice,” Toller said with a touch of sarcasm. There the subject ended.

Farebrother had heard hints before that Lydgate’s spending plainly exceeded the earnings of his practice. Still, he thought it quite possible that other resources or expectations had justified the outlay at his marriage and might prevent the disappointing practice from having serious consequences. One evening he made a special trip to Middlemarch to talk with Lydgate as in earlier days. He noticed a strained excitement quite unlike Lydgate’s usual ease, whether sitting silent or breaking out with sudden energy when he had something to say. In his workroom, Lydgate talked continuously, weighing arguments for and against certain biological theories. Yet he had no definite result to explain or exhibit, none of the landmarks of patient, uninterrupted research on which he himself used to insist. “Every inquiry needs its systole and diastole,” he would say, and “A man’s mind must keep expanding and contracting between the whole human horizon and the field of a microscope lens.” That evening, he seemed to range widely in conversation to prevent it from touching anything personal. Before long they joined Rosamond in the drawing room. Lydgate asked her to play for them, then sank silently into a chair, a strange brightness in his eyes. “Perhaps he’s taken an opiate,” Farebrother thought. “Facial neuralgia, perhaps—or worries about his patients.”

It never occurred to him that Lydgate’s marriage might be anything but happy. Like everyone else, he believed Rosamond sweet-tempered and compliant. He had always found her rather uninteresting, though: a little too much the perfect sample from a finishing school. His mother could not forgive her for seeming never to notice Henrietta Noble’s presence. “Still, Lydgate fell in love with her,” the Vicar told himself, “so she must suit him.”

Farebrother knew Lydgate was proud. But he had so little of that pride himself, and perhaps cared too little about personal dignity apart from avoiding meanness or foolishness, that he could scarcely make enough allowance for Lydgate’s reaction. The prospect of saying a word about his private affairs made Lydgate recoil as if from a burn. Soon after the dinner at Toller’s, the Vicar learned something that made him look still more eagerly for a chance to suggest, indirectly, that if Lydgate ever wanted to discuss a difficulty, a friendly listener was ready.

The chance came at the Vincys’ New Year’s Day party. Farebrother could not resist their invitation: they insisted he must not desert old friends on his first New Year as a greater man, a Rector as well as a Vicar. It was a thoroughly friendly gathering. All the women of the Farebrother household attended, and all the Vincy children ate at the table. Fred had persuaded his mother that leaving out Mary Garth would insult the Farebrothers, since she was their particular friend. Mary came, and Fred was in high spirits, though his enjoyment was mixed. He rejoiced that his mother could see how highly the most important guests valued Mary, but jealousy sharply streaked that triumph whenever Farebrother sat beside her. Fred had felt much easier about his own accomplishments before he began to fear being “bowled out by Farebrother.” The danger still haunted him. Mrs. Vincy, in the full bloom of matronly beauty, looked at Mary’s small figure, coarse wavy hair, and complexion without roses or lilies, and wondered. She tried unsuccessfully to imagine caring how Mary would look in wedding clothes, or taking satisfaction in grandchildren who would look like the Garths. Nevertheless, the party was merry, and Mary particularly lively. For Fred’s sake she was glad his friends were warming to her. She was also quite willing to let them see how much others valued her—people whose judgment they had to respect.

Farebrother noticed that Lydgate looked bored and that Vincy spoke to his son-in-law as little as possible. Rosamond was perfectly composed and graceful. Only a closer scrutiny than the Vicar had felt prompted to give her would have detected the complete absence of the interest a loving wife inevitably shows in her husband’s presence, even when etiquette keeps them apart. When Lydgate joined in the conversation, she looked no more toward him than a statue of Psyche sculpted to face elsewhere. When he returned after being called out for an hour or two, she appeared not to notice an event that eighteen months earlier would have transformed everything, like placing a numeral before a row of zeros. In fact, she was intensely aware of his voice and movements. Her pretty, good-natured air of indifference was a deliberate denial. Through it she satisfied her inward resistance to him while remaining perfectly proper. After Lydgate was called away during dessert, the women went to the drawing room. Rosamond happened to stand near Mrs. Farebrother, who said, “You must do without a great deal of your husband’s company, Mrs. Lydgate.”
“Yes, a doctor’s life is very demanding, particularly when he’s as devoted to his work as Mr. Lydgate.” Having delivered this correct little speech, Rosamond moved away with ease.

“She’s dreadfully lonely when there’s no company,” said Mrs. Vincy, seated beside the old lady. “I certainly thought so when she was ill and I stayed with her. Ours is a cheerful house, Mrs. Farebrother. I’m cheerful by nature, and Mr. Vincy always likes something going on. That’s what Rosamond grew up with. It’s very different having a husband out at all hours, never knowing when he’ll come home, and a reserved, proud sort of man, _I_ think.” Even indiscreet Mrs. Vincy lowered her voice a little for this aside. “But Rosamond has always had an angel’s temper. Her brothers often displeased her, yet she was never one to show it. From babyhood she was as good as could be, and such a complexion! But thank God, all my children are good-tempered.”

Anyone watching Mrs. Vincy toss back her broad cap ribbons and smile toward her three younger daughters, aged seven to eleven, could readily believe her. But that smiling glance had to include Mary Garth. The girls had cornered Mary and made her tell them stories. She was just finishing the delightful tale of Rumpelstiltskin, which she knew by heart because Letty never tired of educating her ignorant elders from a favorite red book. Louisa, her mother’s darling, ran over with wide eyes and solemn excitement. “Oh, Mamma! The little man stamped so hard he couldn’t get his leg out of the floor!”

“Bless you, my little angel!” her mother said. “You can tell me all about it tomorrow. Go back and listen.” Watching Louisa return to that attractive corner, she decided that if Fred wanted Mary invited again, she would not object. The children liked her so much.

Soon the corner grew livelier still. Farebrother came in, sat behind Louisa, and lifted her onto his lap. All the girls insisted he must hear Rumpelstiltskin and Mary must tell it again. He insisted too. Without any fuss, Mary began again in her precise manner, using exactly the same words. Fred had also settled nearby. His pride in Mary’s success would have been complete had Farebrother not watched her with obvious admiration while acting out an intense interest in the tale for the children’s pleasure.
“You won’t want to hear about my one-eyed giant anymore, Loo,” Fred said when she finished.
“Yes, I will. Tell us about him now,” Louisa replied.
“Oh, of course! I’ve been completely replaced. Ask Mr. Farebrother.”

“Yes,” Mary added, “ask him about the ants whose beautiful house was knocked down by a giant called Tom. He thought they didn’t mind because he couldn’t hear them crying or see them using their handkerchiefs.”
“Please?” Louisa asked, looking up at the Vicar.
“No, no. I’m a serious old parson. Whenever I reach into my bag for a story, out comes a sermon. Shall I preach you one?” He put on his spectacles for short-sightedness and pursed his lips.
“Yes,” Louisa said uncertainly.
“Now, let me think. Against cakes: how wicked cakes are, particularly sweet ones with raisins in them.”
Louisa took this rather seriously. She climbed off the Vicar’s knee and went to Fred.

“Ah, I see New Year’s Day isn’t the time for preaching,” Farebrother said, getting up and moving away. He had lately realized that Fred was jealous of him. He had also realized that his own preference for Mary over every other woman was not fading.
“Miss Garth is a delightful young woman,” said Mrs. Farebrother, who had been watching her son.
“Yes,” Mrs. Vincy answered, obliged to reply when the old lady turned toward her expectantly. “It’s a pity she isn’t prettier.”

“I can’t agree,” Mrs. Farebrother said firmly. “I like her face. We mustn’t always demand beauty when a good God has chosen to make an excellent young woman without it. Good manners come first with me, and Miss Garth would know how to behave in any position.”

Her tone was slightly sharp because she was imagining Mary as her daughter-in-law. Mary’s situation with Fred had the disadvantage that it could not appropriately be made public. The three ladies at Lowick Parsonage therefore still hoped Camden would choose Miss Garth.

More visitors arrived. The drawing room was given over to games and music, while whist tables were set up in the quiet room across the hall. Farebrother played a rubber to please his mother. She considered her occasional game a protest against slander and newfangled opinions, which gave dignity even to playing the wrong suit. Afterward he asked Chichely to take his place and left. As he crossed the hall, Lydgate had just arrived and was removing his overcoat.

“You’re just the man I was looking for,” the Vicar said. Instead of going into the drawing room, they walked along the hall and stopped by the fireplace, where the frosty air helped the banked fire glow. Smiling at Lydgate, he continued, “You see how easily I can leave the whist table now that I don’t play for money. Mrs. Casaubon says I owe that to you.”
“How so?” Lydgate asked coldly.

“Ah, you didn’t want me to find out. I call that an ungenerous sort of secrecy. You should allow a man the pleasure of knowing you’ve helped him. I’ve never understood why some people dislike being obliged to others. On my word, I’d rather be obliged to everyone for treating me well.”

“I don’t know what you’re referring to,” Lydgate said, “unless it’s that I once mentioned you to Mrs. Casaubon. But I didn’t expect her to break her promise not to tell you.” He leaned against the corner of the mantel, his face showing no pleasure.

“Brooke let it slip the other day. He paid me the compliment of saying how glad he was I’d got the living, although you’d upset his plans. Apparently you praised me as another Ken or Tillotson and so forth, until Mrs. Casaubon wouldn’t consider anyone else.”
“Brooke is such a loose-tongued fool,” Lydgate said contemptuously.

“Well, I was glad of his loose tongue on that occasion. My dear fellow, I don’t see why you should mind my knowing you wanted to help me. And you certainly have. It puts quite a check on self-satisfaction to discover how much of one’s good behavior depends on having enough money. A man won’t be tempted to say the Lord’s Prayer backward to please the devil if he has no need of the devil’s services. I no longer have to wait on the favors of chance.”
“I don’t see how anyone makes money without chance,” said Lydgate. “If he earns it through a profession, chance is almost certain to be responsible.”
This was so unlike Lydgate’s former way of speaking that Farebrother explained it to himself as the perversity that often grows out of a troubled man’s dark mood. He replied with cheerful agreement—
“Yes, the world’s ways demand an enormous amount of patience. But waiting patiently is easier when a man has friends who love him and want nothing more than to help him through, as far as they can.”
“Oh, certainly,” Lydgate said carelessly, shifting his position and consulting his watch. “People make far more of their difficulties than they need to.”

He understood perfectly that Farebrother was offering to help him, and he could not bear it. Such strange impulses govern us: he had long enjoyed the knowledge that he had privately done the Vicar a service, yet the suggestion that the Vicar now saw his need for a service in return drove him into impenetrable silence. Besides, what must follow such an offer? He would have to “explain his circumstances,” hint that he needed specific things. At that moment, killing himself seemed easier.

Farebrother was too perceptive to miss the meaning of the reply. There was also something massive in Lydgate’s manner and voice, matching his build, which seemed to rule out persuasion once he had rejected an approach.
“What time do you make it?” the Vicar asked, swallowing his hurt.
“Past eleven,” Lydgate replied. They went into the drawing room.
